Besides, there is another thing, too, that is to be considered — that it is no small honor that is conferred upon us, when God glorifies himself in us; for it becomes us to look not so much to life itself, as to the end for which we live.
But on me also, lest I should have sorrow. Paul acknowledges that the death of Epaphroditus would have been bitterly painful to him, and he recognises it as an instance of God’s sparing mercy toward himself, that he had been restored to health. He does not, therefore, make it his boast that he has the apathy (ἀπάθειαν) of the Stoics, as if he were a man of iron, and exempt from human affections.
Calvin, in the French version, makes reference to what he has said on the subject in the Institutes. See Institutes, vol. 2, p. 281. — Ed.
“What then!” some one will say, “where is that unconquerable magnanimity?—where is that indefatigable perseverance?” I answer, that Christian patience differs widely from philosophical obstinacy, and still more from the stubborn and fierce sterness of the Stoics. For what excellence were there in patiently enduring the cross, if there were in it no feeling of pain and bitterness? But when the consolation of God overcomes that feeling, so that we do not resist, but, on the contrary, give our back to the endurance of the rod, (Isaiah 50:5,) we in that case present to God a sacrifice of obedience that is acceptable to him. Thus Paul acknowledges that he felt some uneasiness and pain from his bonds, but that he nevertheless cheerfully endured these same bonds for the sake of Christ.
“Pour l’amour de Christ;” — “From love to Christ.”
He acknowledges that he would have felt the death of Epaphroditus an event hard to be endured, but he would at length have brought his temper of mind into accordance with the will of God, although all reluctance was not yet fully removed; for we give proof of our obedience, only when we bridle our depraved affections, and do not give way to the infirmity of the flesh.
“Ne nous laissons point vaincre par l’infirmite de nostre chair;” — “Do not allow ourselves to be overcome by the infirmity of our flesh.”
Two things, therefore, are to be observed: in the first place, that the dispositions which God originally implanted in our nature are not evil in themselves, because they do not arise from the fault of corrupt nature, but come forth from God as their Author; of this nature is the grief that is felt on occasion of the death of friends: in the second place, that Paul had many other reasons for regret in connection with the death of Epaphroditus, and that these were not merely excusable, but altogether necessary. This, in the first place, is invariable in the case of all believers, that, on occasion of the death of any one, they are reminded of the anger of God against sin; but Paul was the more affected with the loss sustained by the Church, which he saw would be deprived of a singularly good pastor at a time when the good were so few in number. Those who would have dispositions of this kind altogether subdued and eradicated, do not picture to themselves merely men of flint, but men that are fierce and savage. In the depravity of our nature, however, everything in us is so perverted, that in whatever direction our minds are bent, they always go beyond bounds. Hence it is that there is nothing that is so pure or right in itself, as not to bring with it some contagion. Nay more, Paul, as being a man, would, I do not deny, have experienced in his grief something of human error,
“Mesme ie ne nie pas que sainct Paul (comme il estoit homme) ne se trouué surprins de quelque exces vicieux en sa douleur;” — “Nay more, I do not deny that St. Paul (inasmuch as he was a man) might find himself overtaken with some faulty excess in his grief.”
for he was subject to infirmity, and required to be tried with temptations, in order that he might have occasion of victory by striving and resisting.
entries.95f2144050e1ad9fe4929cd25877a238c7a42896: <div annotateRef="Bible:Phil.2.28" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Phil.2.28" sID="gen126628" type="section"/> <div sID="gen126629" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">28</hi> <hi type="italic">I have sent him the more carefully</hi>. The presence of Epaphroditus was no small consolation to him; yet to such a degree did he prefer the welfare of the Philippians to his own advantage, that he says that he rejoices on occasion of his departure, because it grieved him that, on his account, he was taken away from the flock that was intrusted to him, and was reluctant to avail himself of his services, though otherwise agreeable to him, when it was at the expense of loss to them. Hence he says, that he will feel more happiness in the joy of the Philippians.<div eID="gen126629" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Phil.2.28" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen126628" osisID="Phil.2.28" type="section"/>
entries.52c835ebe1dab1ecb40ab88523d6baf5741bfe37: <div annotateRef="Bible:Phil.2.29" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Phil.2.29" sID="gen126630" type="section"/> <div sID="gen126631" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">29</hi> <hi type="italic">Receive him with all joy</hi>. He employs the word <hi type="italic">all</hi> to mean sincere and abundant. He also recommends him again to the Philippians; so intent is he upon this, that all that approve themselves as good and faithful pastors may be held in the highest estimation: for he does not speak merely of one, but exhorts that all such should be held in estimation; for they are precious pearls from God’s treasuries, and the rarer they are, they are so much the more worthy of esteem. Nor can it be doubted that God often punishes our ingratitude and proud disdain, by depriving us of good pastors, when he sees that the most eminent that are given by him are ordinarily despised. Let every one, then, who is desirous that the Church should be fortified against the stratagems and assaults of wolves, make it his care, after the example of Paul, that the authority of good pastors be established; <note n="161"> <div sID="gen126632" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Soit establie et demeure entiere</foreign>;” — “Be established, and remain entire.”<div eID="gen126632" type="x-p"/> </note> as, on the other hand, there is nothing upon which the instruments of the devil are more intent, than on undermining it by every means in their power.<div eID="gen126631" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Phil.2.29" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen126630" osisID="Phil.2.29" type="section"/>
entries.688f6b008f55ac7c3bb2e56a84519640935c52b3:
30 Because for the work of Christ. I consider this as referring to that infirmity, which he had drawn down upon himself by incessant assiduity. Hence he reckons the distemper of Epaphroditus among his excellences, as it certainly was a signal token of his ardent zeal. Sickness, indeed, is not an excellence, but it is an excellence not to spare yourself that you may serve Christ. Epaphroditus felt that his health would be in danger if he applied himself beyond measure; yet he would rather be negligent as to health than be deficient in duty; and that he may commend this conduct the more to the Philippians, he says that it was a filling up of their deficiency,
“Vn accomplissement, ou moyen de suppleer ce qui defailloit de leur seruice;” — “A filling up, or a means of supplying what was defective in their service.”
because, being situated at a distance, they could not furnish aid to Paul at Rome. Hence Epaphroditus, having been sent for this purpose, acted in their stead.
“Faisoit en cest endroit ce qu’ils deuoyent faire;” — “Did in this matter what they ought to have done
He speaks of the services rendered to him as the work of the Lord, as assuredly there is nothing in which we can better serve God, than when we help his servants who labor for the truth of the gospel.
CHAPTER 3
Philippians 3:1-6
1. Finally, my brethren, rejoice in the Lord. To write the same things to you, to me indeed is not grievous, but you it is safe.
1. Quod reliquum est, fratres, mei, gaudete in Domino; eadem scribere vobis, me equidem, haud piget, vobis autem tutm est.
2. Beware of dogs, beware of evil workers, beware of the concision.
2. Videte canes, videte malos operarios, videte concisionem.
3. For we are the cirmcumcision, which worship God in the spirit, and rejoice in Christ Jesus, and have no confidence in the flesh.
3. Nos enim sumus cicrcumcisio, qui spiritu Deum colimus, et gloriamur in Christo Iesu, non autem in carne confidimus.
4. Though I might also have confidence in the flesh. If any other man thinketh that he hath whereof he might trust in the flesh, I more:
4. Tametsi ego etiam in carne fiduciam habeo. Si qauis alius videtur confidere in carne, ego magis:
5. Circumcised the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, an Hebrew of the Hebrews; as touching the law, a Pharisee;
5. Circumcisus die occtavo, ex genere Israel, tribu Beniamin, Hebraeus ex Hebraeis, secundum legem Pharisaeus:
6. Concerning zeal, persecuting the Church; touching the righteousness which is in the law, blameless.
6. Secundum zelum persequens Ecclesiam, secundum iustitiam, quae est in lege, irreprehensibilis.

               <ns0:p n="1">IF <ns0:hi>there be</ns0:hi> therefore any consolation in Christ <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The Apostle reassuming his exhortation in the former Chapter to unanimity, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 27. doth here by way of inference from what went immediately before, press them in a very affectionate manner, with a kind of Rhetorical Relation, and Obtestation as it were adjure them. If any such ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hortation (as the word is rendred, <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 13.15. 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 2, 3. 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 4.13.) in the name of Christ, might avail with them to chear him and one another by their loving concord and being unanimous. Or as we rendring it consolation (so <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 13.15. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 15.4 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 1.4.) <ns0:hi>If</ns0:hi> he which may well sup<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pose and strongly affirm that he took it for granted the main Body of them had in some measure<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> found by his Ministry, what he here moves them to compleat (compare, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 1.6, 7, 27.) in expectation to find more, of what they had experi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mented, what ever indisposition might have crept upon some by the insinuations of the false Apostles, yet, this <ns0:hi>Consolation in Christ</ns0:hi> may be consider'd either (1.) <ns0:hi>Actively q. d.</ns0:hi> If ye would comfort me afflicted, in the concerns of Christ, or if ye have any Christian comfort which doth onely proceed from those that are in Christ, (not from moral Philosophy) or which is wont to be in those who worship the same Christ, let me his Apostle be a partaker thereof. Or (2.) <ns0:hi>Passively,</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 4, 6. <ns0:hi>Philem.</ns0:hi> 7. If you being in Christ, find any consola<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion against your afflictions, for as much as you have received it by my Ministry, we being both in suffering circumstances, should be Farther comforted by a sweet agreement.</ns0:note>, if any comfort of love <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>Syriac</ns0:hi> ren<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der it any speaking to the heart, any Solace from good and com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fortable words did reach your hearts, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 11.19, 31. 1. <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 14.3. 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 2.11. & 5.14 cheared with the love of God or Christ, or the Brethren: or refreshed with my love to you, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 1.8, 9. or would that I should be comforted with your love to me, (as he himself and others were with the gracious affections of the <ns0:hi>Corinthians,</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 7.7.) which ye o<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ght unfeignedly.</ns0:note>, if any fellowship of the Spirit <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">If ye have any Communion with me in the Graces of the Spirit, and stand fast in one Spirit, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 1.27. and would shew that you do persevere in the same Spirit, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 12.4. which acts in all the Members of the Mystical Body of Christ, that do in him their head par<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />take of it.</ns0:note>, if any bowels and mercies <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">If ye are daily affected with any real Sympa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thy, and Commiseration towards me in my bonds for Christ, such inward affections as were moving in him towards them, <ns0:hi>c.</ns0:hi> 1.8. with <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 1.78. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 7.15. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 3.12. the latter word Emphatically expressing the sense of the Metaphor in the former.                <ns0:p n="2">2 Fulfill ye my joy <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> The exercise of those Graces, he had been joyfull for, which would be an Addition to that joy he had for them, and the making of if much more abundant, contributing as much as the Friends of the Bridegrome here can to the compleating of it, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 3.29.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 12.16. & 15.5. 1 Cor. 1.10.</ns0:note> that ye be like min<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ded <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Which is when they believe and affect the same things agreeable to the mind of God, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 3.15. <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 4.32 <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 12.16. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 13.11.</ns0:note>, having the same love <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Ha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ving the same mutual sincere Charity, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 4. 2. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 3.14.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>being</ns0:hi> of one ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cord <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Being unanimous in their honest designs, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 17.22. 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 3.8.</ns0:note>, of one mind <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Agreeing as to the main in the same Judgment and opinion to promote the interest of Christ, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 1.10. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 5.7, 10.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 <ns0:hi>Let</ns0:hi> nothing <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Here the better to engage them to embrace what he had so pathetically exhorted them to, he doth disswade them from animosity, an affectation of applause, and self-seeking; and direct them to modesty and self denial.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>be done</ns0:hi> through strife or vain-glory <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Intimating, they should by no means indulge an inordinate affection to strive and quarrel with one another, provoking each other by an am<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bitious emulation to cross or excell others. This arguing a carnal temper opposite to true Christianity, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 2.8. <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 14. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 5.16, 24, 26. being the very bane of true Christian Concord, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 13.13. <ns0:hi>Iam.</ns0:hi> 3.16. and destructive to Faith, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 5.44. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 12.20.</ns0:note>, but in lowliness of mind let each es<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />teem other better then themselves <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">But cherish and exercise true Christian modesty and meekness (which is of another kind than that the Heathen Philosophers did prescribe) in a due preference of each other, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 11.29. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 12.10. <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 4.2. & 5.21. 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 5.5. as the Apostle himself gave example. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 15.8, 9. <ns0:hi>Q.</ns0:hi> If any say, <ns0:hi>How is this consistant with what the Apostle writes to them to think of praise and good report,</ns0:hi> ch. 4.8. <ns0:hi>and of himself not a whit, and nothing behind the very chiefest Apostles?</ns0:hi> 2 Cor. 11.5. &. 12.11. <ns0:hi>and farther, how can some think others better than themselves in truth, unless they reckon good evil and evil good</ns0:hi>? I answer (1.) Be sure Christian modesty and real Humility, with prudence and mildness, are very commendable Graces, and in the sight of God of great price. 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 3, 4. And therefore what he doth afterwards exhort to in this Epistle, doth very well agree with what he doth write here. Where (2.) He is treating of Grace and Godliness, whereas in those places to the <ns0:hi>Corin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thians,</ns0:hi> he writes of some certain gifts, which by reason of the insinuations of false Apostles against him, he was necessita<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted in magnifying of his Apostolical Office and Authority (2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 10.8.) to mention, being as it were, compell'd to it, by the ingratitude of some of them at <ns0:hi>Corinth</ns0:hi> who had been influenc'd by the false Apostles, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 12.5.6. yet you may see there, he doth not glory of himself, or his Person, but acknowledge his infi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                     </ns0:gap>mities, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 11.30. and that un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />feignedly, speak the truth, every where, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 12.6. which he makes evident to them from the nature of the thing it self, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 10.12, 13, 15, 16. & 12.12. appealing to God, as witness in the case, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 11.31. referring all the glorying they put him upon, to the Grace of God through Christ, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 15.10. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 11.31. when they had cast contempt on his Ministry, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 10.10, 11, 12, 13, 18. So that in respect of gifts and external Privileges, wherein are distinction of Superiours and Inferiours, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 3.4. he doth not urge that every Christian should prefer every other to himself, wherein 'tis e<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vident there is a real difference: but in respect of the Per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sons the honesty and piety of others in God's sight (le<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>t a Man by thinking himself something when he is nothing, should deceive himself, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 6.3.) Sith in his Judgment they may be endow'd with some hidden quality, we know not of, and be accepted with him. Hence (3.) Our Estimation and preference of others to our selves who as Christian Brethren are oblig'd to serve one another, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 5.13. is not taken sim<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ply, and with an absolute Judgment, as if it were necessary to give them the preheminence in all things: but as to this, that a Man may think there is some defect in himsef, which it may be is not in another; or with a suspension perhaps he is not better in truth; but considering mine heart is deceitfull, and possibly he may be more without guile, I judge it not meet to prefer my self to him God-ward: but seeing mine own black Legs, and being bound in love to confess mine own, and cover the infirmities of my Brother, who labours to walk answerable to his profession; 'tis safe for me to pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fer him who may have some good Latent which I have not, and whereupon he is to be esteemed by me. Wherefore (4.) The right management of the duty which the Apostle calls for to preserve Unanimity, depends upon a right and due Estimation of God's divers gifts and Graces which flow from the same Spirit, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 12.4. and an humble sense of our own infirmities: so that however one Christian may excell with some singular endowments: yet he ought to think they were not bestow'd upon him, that he should be puff'd up, or value himself above what is meet upon that account be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore God, being he hath receiv'd them of God, 1. <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 4.7. but judge himself for his own defectiveness and faultiness; which will aford himself matter of abasement and humility; when yet with respect to others, whose hearts he knows not, he in charity thinketh the best, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 13.4, 5. and if in this case he should be mistaken, his modest apprehensi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons would be acceptable to God, (designing to approve that which he doth) and profitable to himself.</ns0:note>.<ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">To en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gage them further unto Christian concord, he here directs them as to their aim and scope (according to the import of the word) that it should not be their own private interest but the common good of Christianity, becoming those who have true Christian love, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 10.24. & 13.5. not as if he did dissallow providing for their own, 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 5.8. or stu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dying to be quiet, and doeing their own business, 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 4.11. but that every member of Christ, whiles he considers his own Gifts, Graces, honour and advantage, would remember that he is not born onely to serve himself or Pharisaically to conceit well of himself in the contempt of others, <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 18.11. but also and that much rather he should consider his re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lation to the head, and every other member of the Body, and so consult the Gifts, Graces, Honour, and Edification of others, especially when more eminently usefull, knowing that members should have the same care one for another, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 12.24, to 28.</ns0:note>

               <ns0:p n="5">5 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Pet. 2.21. 1 Joh. 2.6.</ns0:note> Let <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Most Translations do express the causal or rather illative <ns0:hi>Greek,</ns0:hi> Particle, which ours doth here omit as an expletive. However the Apostle doth urge them to the exercise of self denial, mutual love, and an hearty condescention to one ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther from the great example of Jesus Christ, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 8, 9.</ns0:note> this mind be in you <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">That so the mind which was in Christ, may be perceived in us, who if spiritual judge all things and have the mind of Christ, being enlightn'd by the same Spirit, we do judge as he coming in the flesh did, or, Let the same affection be found in you, that was really in him, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 11.28. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 13.15.</ns0:note> which was al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />so in Christ Jesus.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 Who <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Who,</ns0:hi> i. e. Relative to Christ Jesus, the Eternal Son of God by Nature, very God extant with his Father before the beginning, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 1.1. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 4.4. 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 3.16. & 6.14, 15, 16.<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:hi>Tit.</ns0:hi> 2.13. the express Image and Character of his Father's Person, which implies a peculiar subsistence distinct from the subsistence of his Father, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 8.42. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 4.4. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 1.15. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 1.3. concerning whom, every word that follows by reason of the <ns0:hi>Socinians,</ns0:hi> and some <ns0:hi>Lutherans</ns0:hi> is to be well weighed.</ns0:note>

                     </ns0:gap> 1.1, 2.</ns0:note> being <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e. Subsisting</ns0:hi> in opposition to taking or as<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />suming, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 7. and therefore doth firmly prove Christ, pre-ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />isting in another Nature, to his so doing, namely his ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tual existing of himself in the same essence and Glory, he had from Eternity with the Father, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 1.1, 2. & 17.5.2. <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 8.9. <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 1.4, 8, 11.</ns0:note> in the form of God <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">To understand which clearly (1.) The word <ns0:hi>form,</ns0:hi> though it may sometime note somewhat outward, and so infer the Glory of Christ's Miracles, yet we do not find it any where so used in Scripture: 'tis true it is once used there for the outward visage, <ns0:hi>Mar.</ns0:hi> 16.12. which had excelling splendour and beauty, giving occasion to con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceive Majesty in the Person, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 17.2. 2 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 1 16. (however his resplendent Garments could not be accounted <ns0:hi>the form of God</ns0:hi>) yet being, <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> saith <ns0:hi>c.</ns0:hi> 24.16. The Eyes of the Persons which saw were holden, that for a time they could not acknowledge him, it argues that the appearance, <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> speaks of, noted onely an <ns0:hi>accidental form.</ns0:hi> Whereas the <ns0:hi>being</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>subsisting Paul</ns0:hi> here speaks of, respects (what the best <ns0:hi>Philosophers</ns0:hi> in their most usual way of speaking, do) the <ns0:hi>Essential form</ns0:hi> with the Glory of it, sith the Verbs in other Scriptures of the same Origine, signifie somewhat <ns0:hi>in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ward</ns0:hi> and not conspicuous, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 12.2. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 3.18. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 4.19. especially when there is a cogent reason for it here, con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sidering the <ns0:hi>form of God,</ns0:hi> in opposition to the <ns0:hi>form of a Ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vant</ns0:hi> afterward, and in conjunction with equality to God which implies the same essence and Nature, <ns0:hi>Is.</ns0:hi> 40 25. & 46.5. it being impossible there should be any proportion or e<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quality 'twixt infinite, and finite; eternal, and temporal; increase, and create; by nature God, and by nature not God, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 4.4, 8. unto which the onely living and true God, will not suffer his Glory to be given. Neither indeed can he deny himself who is <ns0:hi>one,</ns0:hi> and besides whom there is no o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther true God, or God by Nature, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 4.35. & 6.4. 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 2.13. who onely doth wondrous things, <ns0:hi>Ps.</ns0:hi> 72.18. For to all Divine Operations, a Divine power is requi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />site which is inseparable from the most simple essence and its properties, <ns0:hi>Being, or subsisting in the form of God,</ns0:hi> imports not Christ's appearance in exerting of God's power, but his real and actual existence in the Divine essence, not in accidents wherein nothing doth subsist, neither the vulgar nor Learned do use to say any one doth subsist, but appear in an outward habit, why then should any conceit the Apostle means so? The <ns0:hi>Gentiles</ns0:hi> might speak of their Gods ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pearing; but then, even they thought the Deity was one thing, and the habit or figure under which, or in which it appear'd was another, <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 14.11. so that <ns0:hi>subsisting in the form</ns0:hi> intimates in the Nature, and essence of God, not bare<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly, but as it were clothed with properties and Glory. For the Apostle here treats of Christ's Condescension, proceeding from his actual existence, as the term wherein he is Co-eter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nal and Co-equal to God the Father, before he abated him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self with respect unto us. For he says not the <ns0:hi>form of God</ns0:hi> was in Christ, (however that might be truly said) that the Adver<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />saries might not have occasion to say onely there was some<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />what in Ch<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ist like unto God, but he speaks of that wherein Christ was, <ns0:hi>viz. in the form of God,</ns0:hi> and so that form is predicated of God, as his essence and nature and can be no o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther thing. None can rationally imagine that God was an external figure, wherein Christ was subsisting. For subsis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tence implies some peculiarity relating to the substance of a certain thing, whence we may conclude the Son to be of the same, (not onely of like) substance with the Father, con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sidering what signantly follows.</ns0:note>, thought it <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>He thought it not,</ns0:hi> es<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />teemed, counted, held, (so the word is us'd, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 3. <ns0:hi>c.</ns0:hi> 3. 7, 8. 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 5.13. & 3.15. 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 1.12. & 6.1. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 10.29. & 11.26.) it not <ns0:hi>Robbery,</ns0:hi> it being his right by eternal Genera<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion) <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> He did not judge it any wrong or usurpation, on that account of his <ns0:hi>being in the form of God,</ns0:hi> to be equal to his Father, being a <ns0:hi>subsistent</ns0:hi> in the same nature and essence with him. From openly shewing equal Majesty with whom he did not for a time abstain, in that he could reckon this Robbery, as if such Majesty were that which did not agree to his nature, ever presupposing this inherent right, to his great condescension, or abusing himself, which follows as the <ns0:hi>term to which</ns0:hi>: or he resolv'd for a time not to shew himself in that glory which was his own right, but freely condescen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ded to the vailing of it. He did not really foregoe (neither was it possible he should) any thing of his Divine Glory, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing the Son of God still, without any Robbery or Rapine, equal to his Father in Power and Glory, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 10.3. & 1. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 5.7, 20.</ns0:note> not robbery <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> doth not say (as the <ns0:hi>A<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ians</ns0:hi> of Old would pervert his sense) he robbed not, or snatched not, held not fast equality with God, or (as the <ns0:hi>Socinians</ns0:hi> since) Christ thought not to doe this Robbery to God, or comm<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>t this Rape upon God, so as that he should be equal to him, but acknowledg'd he had it of the free Gift of God, chopping in the Adversative particle, [<ns0:hi>but</ns0:hi>] where it really is not; whereas we read not in the sacred Text, <ns0:hi>he thought not to do this robbery</ns0:hi>; but <ns0:hi>he thought it not robbery</ns0:hi> to be equal to God; which two are vastly different (even as mu<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>h as to have the God-head by <ns0:hi>usurpation,</ns0:hi> and to have it by <ns0:hi>na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture</ns0:hi>) In the <ns0:hi>former</ns0:hi> 'tis, <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> Christ did not rob or snatch away the equality; in the <ns0:hi>latter,</ns0:hi> the equality which Christ had with God, he thought it no Robbery; he reputed not the Empire, he might have always continued in the exer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cise of, equal with the Father, as a thing usurp'd, or taken by force, (as one doth hold that he hath taken by spoil, making shew of it) For when he had said he had subsisted in the Form of God, he could (before he condescended) say also, he was equal to God, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> the Father, without any Robbery, Rapine or Usurpation. And if <ns0:hi>Socinus</ns0:hi> urge that it is absurd and false in any sense to say, God thought he had robb'd, or taken by robbery the Divine Essence; then this contradictory, God thought not he took by robbery the Di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vine Essence, is rational and true; as when it is said, <ns0:hi>God cannot lye,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>God changeth not,</ns0:hi> as 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 15.29. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 55.8. <ns0:hi>Mal.</ns0:hi> 3.6. What things are denied of God, do not imply the opposites are affirmed of him. The particle [<ns0:hi>But</ns0:hi>] which follows in its proper place before, <ns0:hi>made him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self of no reputation,</ns0:hi> may be fairly joined with this sense. For if Christ should know that by rapine and unjust usurpation he was equal to God, (as likely the attempt to be so, was the Sin of our first Parents, which robbery of theirs Christ came to expiate) he had not emptied himself, nor vouchsafed to abase himself.</ns0:note> to be equal with God <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Neither is Christ said to be equal to God onely <ns0:hi>in respect</ns0:hi> of his works (which yet argue the same cause and principle, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 5.19, 21, 23, 26, 29. & 10.37.) but <ns0:hi>absolutely</ns0:hi> he thought it not robbery to be altogether e<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />qual with God, as subsisting in the same nature and essence, the original phrase connoting an exact Parity. All the things of Christ (though he chose to have some of them vail'd for a time) are equal to God, so some expound the Neuter plu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ral emphatically (as usual amongst the <ns0:hi>Greeks</ns0:hi>) to answer the Masculine singular foregoing, to express the ineffable same<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness of the nature and essence of the divine subsistents. It may be read, He counted it no robbery that those things which are his own should be equal to God, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> the Father; or rather, that he himself should in all things be Equal or Peer to God. For had Christ been onely equal by a delegated power from God, why should the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> have consulted to kill him, for making himself equal with God? which with them was all one, as to make himself God, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 5.18. & 10.33. But that he spake of his eternal Generati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on, as owning him for his own Father, with whom he did work Miracles, even as the Father did in his own name, by his own power, of himself, for his own glory: neither will the <ns0:hi>Evangelist</ns0:hi>'s saying, <ns0:hi>The Son can do nothing of him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self,</ns0:hi> infer an inequality with the Father, when what he doth, is equally perfect in power, and glory with the Father's, whence as Son, he hath it by nature. For (looking lower) though every Son receives from his Father, humane nature; yet is he not less a Man than his Father, or his Father more a Man than he; The Son having a being of the same per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fection which is naturally in both; however the Father <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>o whom Christ is in subordination as the Son, and in Office a Servant, undertaking the work of Mediation, may be said to be greater than the Son, that can onely be understood with respect to the <ns0:hi>order</ns0:hi> of their working, if we compare Texts, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 14.28. & 16.13, 14, 15. Neither when Christ accounted it not robbery to be equal with God, is he said (as the Adversaries urge) to be equal to himself, but to ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther person, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> God the Father. Things may be equal which are so divers, that yet they may be one in some common res<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pect wherein they agree: wherefore when Christ is said to be equal with the Father, he is distinguished from him in Person and Subsistence, yet not in Essence, wherein it is his due to be his equal, and therefore One.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:495" />7 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal 22.6.</ns0:note> But <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Some expound this <ns0:hi>particle</ns0:hi> as a Discretive, others an Adversative, or Redditive.</ns0:note> made himself <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Most wittingly emptied him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self, or abated himself of the all fulness of glory he had e<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />qually with God the Father, that considering the dispro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />portion betwixt the Creature and the Creatour; he in the eyes of those, amongst whom he tabernacled, appear'd to have nothing of reputation left him, <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 9.26. 'Tis not said the <ns0:hi>Form of God</ns0:hi> was cut off, or did empty it self: but he who did suffer <ns0:hi>in</ns0:hi> the Form of God, made himself of no account; did empty, abate, or abase himself, (so the A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />postle elsewhere Actively and Passively useth the word, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 9.15. with 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 9.3.) and that indeed whiles <ns0:hi>subsisting in</ns0:hi> the Form of God (according to agreement, <ns0:hi>Zach.</ns0:hi> 6.13. & 1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.7.) not by laying aside the nature of God, but in some other way, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> his own way, kept secret till he was pleased to manifest it, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 16.25. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 1.26. by freely coming in the fle<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>h, 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 3.16. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 10.7. which is such an asto<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nishing wonder, and mysterious abasement, as gains the greatest veneration from his Saints. Thus for a little time laying aside, at his own pleasure withdrawing, and going a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />side from his glorious Majesty. He lessen'd himself for the Salvation of his People. He had a liberty not to shew his Majesty, Fulness, and Glory during his pleasure, so that he could (as to our eyes) contract and shadow it, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 1.14. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 2.9. His condescension was free, and unconstrained with the consent of his Father, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 3.13. so that though the Scripture saith, The <ns0:hi>most high</ns0:hi> dwelleth not in Temples made with hands; yet the Son of the Highest, 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 8.27. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 66.1. <ns0:hi>Mark.</ns0:hi> 5.7. <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 7.48. can at his own pleasure shew, or eclipse his own glorious brightness, abate or let out his fulness, exalt or abase himself in respect of us. How<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ever in his own simple and absolute nature, he be without va<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />riableness or shadow of turning, <ns0:hi>Iam.</ns0:hi> 1.17. <ns0:hi>being</ns0:hi> his Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers equal, and so abides most simple and immutable: yet respectively to his state, and what he had to manage for the Redemption of lost Man; with regard to the discovery he made of himself in the revelation of his Divine Properties, the acknowledgment and celebration of them, by the Crea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tures, he emptied himself, not by ceasing to be what he was before, equal with his Father, or laying down the essential Form of God, according to which he was equ<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>l to God; but by <ns0:hi>taking the form of a servant,</ns0:hi> wherein he was like to Men, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> assuming something to himself he had not before, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> the humane nature; vailing himself, as the Sun is said to be vailed, not in it self, but in regard of the intervening Cloud, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 27.39. to 45. what could hinder that he should not manifest his excellency now more, then less clearly? Men one while acknowledging and praising it, another while neither acknowledging or praising of it, then again praising of it, yet more sparingly? He by taking the form of a mean Man, might so obscure the dignity of his Person, as to the acknowledgement of him to be the Son of God, equal with his Father, that in vouching himself to be so, he might be accounted a Blasphemer, <ns0:hi>Iob.</ns0:hi> 10.36. and during that ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pearance, not seem to <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> the most high; even as a King by laying aside the tokens of his Royalty, and putting on the habit of a Merchant, when all the while he ceaseth not to be King, or the highest in his own Dominions. Hence the <ns0:hi>most high</ns0:hi> may be considered, either in regard of his nature, where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />in he holdeth the highest degree of perfection; or in regard of those personal act<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> he performs in the business of our Salvation. In the former, Christ is the most High; in the latter, our Mediatour. So the Form of God was the <ns0:hi>term from which,</ns0:hi> and the Form of a Servant, the <ns0:hi>term to which,</ns0:hi> he mov'd in his demission, or abasement, which did not simply lie in an assumption or union of the Humane Nature to the Divine, for this doth abide still in Christ highly exal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted, but in taking the form of a Servant, which with the humane Nature he took, by being sent forth, made of a Woman under the Law, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 4.4. but by his Resurrection and Glorification, lest that Relation or Habit of a Servant (being such an one who was also a Son, and a Lord, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 1.2. with 3.6.) when yet he retains the humane Nature still. As therefore he was of the Seed of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> according to the Flesh; <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1.3. though before he had not flesh: so he took the form of a Servant in the likeness of Man, according to his humane Na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture, although before he took that Form, he could not have humane Nature: He did not annihilate any thing he was be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore; onely of his own accord, bowed down himself, and va<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

               <ns0:p n="9">9 Wherefore <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Some take this particle <ns0:hi>illatively</ns0:hi> connoting the consequent of Christ's Exaltation, upon his antecedent humiliation, as elsewhere, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 10.17. <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 20.26. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 3.7. 2 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 1.10. This the <ns0:hi>Aethiopic</ns0:hi> version favors, Christ respecting not himself, but us, and our good, the Glory that he had eternally but vailed for a time, emer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ging (as the Sun out of a Cloud) upon his finishing the work his Father gave him to doe, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 17.5. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 9.5. O<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers take the particle <ns0:hi>causally</ns0:hi> intimating Christ's meriting his own exaltation and our Salvation, and his accepting of superexcellent Glory as a reward of his unparallel'd obedience, though he might have challeng'd it, by virtue of the personal union, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 13.20. with 12.2. obedience superiour to An<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gels, required a recompence superiour to their Glory, and Christ might upon his exquisite obedience, demand his own mediatory Glory as being our Head, and that being the be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ginning and cause of ours. However whether the particle of order note that of consequence, or causality, or both, there is no need of controversie (because of the Communication of properties) sith the Person of Christ, as God-man was glori<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fi'd.</ns0:note> God also hath highly exalted him <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> elegancy imports superexalted, or ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />alted with all exaltation, answering to his gradual humiliation above the grave in his Resurrection, the earth in his Ascensi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on and above the Heavens, at his Fathers right hand, upon the Throne of his Glory, to judge the world, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 1.20, 21. & 4.10.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Heb. 1.4.</ns0:note> given him a name <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Some take <ns0:hi>name</ns0:hi> literally restraining it to <ns0:hi>Iesus,</ns0:hi> but those letters and syllables are not above every name, <ns0:hi>Ez<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ra</ns0:hi> 2.2. & 10.18. <ns0:hi>Hagg.</ns0:hi> 1.1. <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 7.45. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 4.11. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 4.8. it being common to others, though upon a different account it was to Christ, even before his incarnation, <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 1.31. Others for the name of the onely begotten Son of God the Father, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 1.14. (with <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 1.4. & 5.8.) who was more eminently manifested in his exaltation, to Angels and to Men, than before. Others not for any Title but the thing consequent upon his humiliation, surpassing that of all Crea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tures, Potentates on Earth, and Angels in Heaven, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 1.20, 21. Name imports power, <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 3.6. &. 4.7. <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 5.12. of the Christ, the Saviour, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 12.21. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 4.42. <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 4.11, 12. & 10.42. at God's right hand where he living to inter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cede makes all comfortable to us, who in his name alone do be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lieve, pray, praise, and doe all that shall find acceptance, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 18.20. & 28.19. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 1.12. & 3.18. & 14.13. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 10.13, 14. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 3.17. Power to confer all for the good of his Church being given him, upon his Death, when with respect to the creatures he receiv'd a glory, not in regard of himself, and in it self, but in regard of its patefaction to others, from which glory during the time of his humiliation, he had by a voluntary dispensation abstain'd; and the exercise of that Authority confer'd upon him as Mediatour, in that humane Nature, he had so obediently subjected himself to the Cross. Though as God, there was a manifestation, yet there was no intrinsecal addition of Glory. He did as Man receive the name, or glory he had from all Eternity as God. So that the name or Glory given relates to him according to both natures as Mediatour God-man: not as God, so he could not be exalted at all, being the most high, not as meer Man, so a Creature is not capable of Divine Worship, which in what follows is expresly required to be given to him, who is superexalted by God's right Hand, above every name, and every thing known by any name, <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 2.24, 33, 36. & 5.31. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 15 25. <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 17.14. with 19.16.</ns0:note>, which is above every name:</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 45.23.</ns0:note> That at <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">In the Old Translation by Bishops in Queen <ns0:hi>Eliza<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />beth</ns0:hi>'s time, (and some say in the Manuscripts of this) it is <ns0:hi>in</ns0:hi> the Name.                   </ns0:note> the name of Jesus <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">But constructively of Jesus, intimating, that the Power, Glory, and Majesty of him who hath that name, unto which every knee is bowed, is that name which is above every name; which would not hold true, if the name were took for the very word <ns0:hi>Iesus,</ns0:hi> (that as before) being common to others in <ns0:hi>Hebrew, Greek, and Latin,</ns0:hi> yea, and <ns0:hi>English.</ns0:hi> Besides neither in letters, nor syllables, nor sound, nor time, hath that word any thing above other words.</ns0:note>, every knee should bow <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Bowing of the knee,</ns0:hi> is meant <ns0:hi>Metonymically,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Metaphorically,</ns0:hi> because some of those hereafter named, from whom the Homage is due, have neither Knees nor Tongues, yet must either willingly, or by constraint, yield subjection and obedience to the Sovereign Authority of Christ here, and hereafter, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 11.27. & 28.18. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 5.22, 23. <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 3.15. all Creatures being made subject to him, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 2.8.                   <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:496" />11 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 13.13.</ns0:note> that every tongue <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">By <ns0:hi>tongue,</ns0:hi> not onely every Language, People, and Nation is meant; because 'tis to be understood, as before particularized of Angels aswell as Men, for though Angels properly, and by nature want <ns0:hi>tongues,</ns0:hi> (aswell as <ns0:hi>knees,</ns0:hi> which are both here joined, and must not be sever'd in the Wor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ship given to Christ) yet in their manner of speaking to Men, under an extraordinary dispensation, they may use them, (or that which is equivalent) 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 13.1. and in a way proper to them.</ns0:note> should confess that Jesus Christ <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> Lord <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Can <ns0:hi>confess,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>express</ns0:hi> their adoration of Christ, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 7.9, 11, 12. either with delight, or by a forc't subjection, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 6.16. and acknowledge that he is Lord, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> of glory, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 11.36. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 2.8. & 8.6. the Son of God, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 4.5. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 1.2, 4. having onely power to command the Soul, and Conscience, <ns0:hi>Iam.</ns0:hi> 4.12. and to save, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 7.25. being Lord both of the dead, and of the living, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 14.9.</ns0:note>, to the glory of God the Father.<ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Some render <ns0:hi>in</ns0:hi> the glory of the Father. Either in that, the honour of Christ redoundeth to the honour of the Father, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 10.1. with <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 5.23. <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 1.6. or the Father doth most glorifie the Son in his Exaltation, who had most glorified him in his Humiliation, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 12.28. with 17.5, 6.</ns0:note>

               <ns0:p n="12">12 Wherefore my beloved <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">Having confirmed the example of Christ's admirable Condescension, and affection from the glorious issue of it, he doth here reassume his exhortation, with a friendly com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pellation.</ns0:note> as ye have al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ways obeyed <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Commending their former sincere endeavours to obey the Gospel (so, <ns0:hi>c.</ns0:hi> 1.5. & <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 15. of this) in following Christ, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 11.28. and moving them to persevere in obe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dience and love to God, and Man.</ns0:note>, not as in my presence onely, but now much more in my absence <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">That it might be e<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vident whether the Eye of their Pastour were upon them or no, a prevailing love to Christ, and their own Souls welfare, was prevalent with them, but especially being he was now detain'd from them, and might be jealous of some defects in them, <ns0:hi>Iam.</ns0:hi> 3.2. 1 <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 1.8. did engage them more than a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ny thing to embrace his Exhortation, which he enlargeth in other words.</ns0:note>; work out your own salvation <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">He moves them as Saints, <ns0:hi>c.</ns0:hi> 1.1. in whom God would perfect his work, begun, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 6. having given to them to believe and suffer, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 29. that they would seriously and earnestly busie themselves in those things, which on their parts are necessary to Salvation as, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 6.27. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 6.9. and without which it cannot be had as, <ns0:hi>c.</ns0:hi> 1.10. <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 24.13. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 3.10, 12, &c. 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 1.18, 19. & 6.19. 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 2.5. & 4.7, 8. 2 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 3.17. yea press on in the way to their own Salvation, (as he mov'd, 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 4.16.) not that they should not be solicitous about others, for that mutual care is imply'd as elsewhere requir'd, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 3.13. & 10.24. but that every one should strenuously go on towards the mark with a special regard to himself, and the Temptations, he may meet with, knowing he must bear his own burthen, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 6.1, 3. and therefore should take heed lest he fall. The <ns0:hi>Papists</ns0:hi> arguings hence that our actions are efficient and me<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ritorious causes of Salvation, are altogether inconsequent. For the Apostle doth not say our actions work out Salvation, but work ye out your own Salvation, which is much different. 'Twere absurd to say because the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> were enjoyn'd to eat the Passover with Loins girt, that Loins girt were eating of the Passover. Indeed what the <ns0:hi>Papists</ns0:hi> urge is contrary to this Doctrine of <ns0:hi>Paul,</ns0:hi> who doth elsewhere place blessedness in remission of Sins, and shews eternal life, is the gift of God, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 4.6, 7. & 6.23. and we are sav'd by grace not of works, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 3.20, 24.25. & 4.16. <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 2.8. <ns0:hi>Tit.</ns0:hi> 3.5. and contrary to the main scope of the Apostle, which is to beat down pride, and conceit of deserving, and perswade to humility, he drives at this, that we should not be idle or lazie in the bu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />siness of Salvation, but work together with God, (yet as in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />struments in whom there is no strength which is not deriv'd from him) that we may evidence we do not receive his grace in vain, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 6.1, 2. But this co-operation doth not respect the acquiring or meriting of Salvation which is proper to Christ alone, and incommunicable to any others, <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 4.12. who cannot be said to be their own Saviours: this Co-ope<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ration or <ns0:hi>working out</ns0:hi> respects onely the application, not the performing of the payment, which Christ hath abundantly perfected: but the embracing of the perfect payment, is not that which can be the cause and foundation of right for which it is deservedly confer'd: but onely the way and means by which we come to partake of Salvation.</ns0:note>, with fear, and trembling <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> with an ho<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly care to doe all acceptably; he doth by these two words mean not any servile fear and slavish despondence arising from doubting, <ns0:hi>c.</ns0:hi> 4.4. but onely a serious filial fear implying a deep humility and submissiveness of mind, with a reverential awe of the divine Majesty and a solicitude, to avoid that evil which is offensive to him and separates from him. We find these words used to the like import, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 2.11. <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 5.19. & 6.26. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 11.20. with 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 2.3. & 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 7.5. <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 6.5. connoting that after the example of Christ, we should be humble, and though we distrust in our selves, yet we are to trust solely to God, (as an infant may be affraid and cling yet fast to, and depend upon, begging help of the parent going over a dangerous precipice) for the acomplishment of our Sal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vation.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 For <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">That they might not be negligent in working out their Salvation with humility, from any conceit, or carnal confi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dence any might have that they could believe and repent when they pleased, imagining their wills to be as pliable to good as evil: the Apostle urgeth the effectual grace of God, as a powerfull enducement and encouragement to em<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />brace his exhortation.</ns0:note> it is God <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">They should not despond of any attaining Salvation, or think they did labour in vain, in the diligent use of means, and should altogether fall under the dominion of sin, considering though they were free Agents, yet the efficiency and sufficiency was of God, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 6.13, 14. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 4.7. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 3.5.</ns0:note> which worketh in you <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Who worketh within them powerfully, and effectually, carrying on the work through all difficulties and obstacles, with victori<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ous efficacy till it be wrought, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 1.6. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 41.4. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 13.21. God working not onely by suasion to gain assent, but by a special energie effecting what he would have us to doe.</ns0:note>, both to will <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">And not onely in a general way, <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 17.28. but in a special way making us willing, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 110.3. re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />motely in regard of the principle, nextly in regard of the act: circumcising the heart, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 30.6. taking away the heart of stone, and giving an heart of flesh, <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 11.19. & 36.26, 27. causing light to shine out of darkness, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 4.6. and so renewing the will, to chuse that which is savingly good, the natural bent of which before the in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fluence of this insuperable grace, stands another way, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 8.44. <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> to will, and doe contrary: yet he doth not necessitate by any compulsion, but powerfully, yet sweetly, and suitably to Man's free faculty, encline the will to that which is good, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 6.37, 44. <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> to a certain effect. For the will influenced to will that it doth perform,, it un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />doubtedly wills somewhat that is certain, and so is deter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mined by God.</ns0:note>, and to doe <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">To doe that which is savingly good. Whereupon being made willing, it hath not onely an in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />clination, and doth not onely exert a woulding, but being moved by God's insuperable grace, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 3.7. that will is effectual, and is the very deed, where the command of the will is executed to the glory of God, as the Au<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thour. As in Alms, not onely doth God incline the will to relieve the Poor, but further contributes special gra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cious aids to perform what was deliberated, which evin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceth, that it is from another principle than our selves. It is not, that ye may be able to will, and may be able to doe: but he worketh both to will, and to doe: which connotes the very act it self: that ye will, to believe, obey, pray, persevere; and that ye do belive, obey, pray, persevere: of unwilling, he makes willing; and further, to will, and to doe. 'Tis true, to will, as it is an act of the will, is ours by Creation; and to will well is so far ours, we be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing made effectually willing by God's grace: yet not ours, as though of our selves we begin to will, or go on, but it is of him who worketh in us. Not that we cannot will well, but that of our selves we cannot will well. The precept therefore requiring our obedience does not shew what we can or will of our selves, but what we ought to will and to doe, by God's special help. But though God work in us obedience; yet we obey, we our selves act, being acted of God.</ns0:note>, of <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> good pleasure <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Not for any previous disposition in any of us, but of, or accor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ding to his own good pleasure, <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 10.21. <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 1.5, 9, 11. & 2.8. 2 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 1.11. with 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 1.9. In work<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing out our own Salvation, the very beginning in the will, aswell as the perfection is ascribed to the efficacy of God: his good pleasure is the procreating and helping cause of this work on the will, and not the wills good pleasure.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
