He doth not say, holding forth carnal institutions, nor humane traditions; but that word, where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />in is to be had Eternal Life, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 5.39. & 6.68.</ns0:note>; <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">2 Cor. 1.14.</ns0:note> that I may rejoyce in the day of Christ <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Quick<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ning them from the consideration of the glorious joy he should have in their Salvation, at the day of Christ, see <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 1.6. when he and they should of God's free Grace, receive an abundant reward, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> of his Ministry and Ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hortation, and of their embracing it, and working out their Salvation by God's special assistance.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Gal. 2.2.</ns0:note> that I have not run in vain, neither laboured in vain <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">For it would be evident to his, aswell as their everlasting comfort, when he should see them, that his laborious Ministry a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mongst them had not been frustrate, or fruitless in the Lord, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 25.21. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 3.8, 9. & 15.58. Then in a more glorious way, they would be his Joy and Crown, than they were at present, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 4.1.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 Yea and if <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">That he might further confirm and encourage them in their Duty, he doth not here conclude the certainty of his death, at his first imprisonment, having expressed be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore some confidence of his surviving it, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 1.19, 25. but in imitation of Christ, the good Shepherd, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 10.11. to demonstrate his constant affection to them (as he doth to others, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 12.15. 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 2.8.) he argues upon supposition of his own death, which might afterwards hap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pen, 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 4.6.</ns0:note> I be <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gr. <ns0:hi>powred forth or a drink offering.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> offered <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Using an elegant Alegory, borrow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed from legal Offerings, <ns0:hi>Lev.</ns0:hi> 2.6. <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 15.5, 7. & 23.7. <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 9.13. to shew that he could cheerfully lay down his life for their Salvation, not for reconci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ling them to God, for that was done before by Christ's own offering up himself, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 7.27. a Sacrifice of a sweet smell unto God, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 5.2. but whereby they might be confirmed in the Faith sealed with his Bloud, for bearing Witness to Christ, pretious to God, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 116.15. The <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> word he hath here, is borrowed from the usage in Sacrificing, of pouring Wine, or Oil upon the victim, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 30.9. 2 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 16.13. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 19.13. when that which was poured forth was called the Drink-offering, to the confirming of Covenants.</ns0:note> upon the sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />crifice <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">By Sacrifice, he means either specially their Alms, prepared by them, and pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sented by <ns0:hi>Epaphroditus,</ns0:hi> for supporting him in his sufferings, and in the Person of the Apostle offered up unto God, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 4.18. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 9.12. or more generally, the <ns0:hi>Philippians</ns0:hi> Conversion, because sanctified by a princi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple of Faith, and so made a Sacrifice. For he doth more than once write of Believers being offered, and resigned to God, under the notion of a Sacrifice, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 12.1. & 15.16. and so doth another, 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 2.5.</ns0:note> and service <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">To bring them unto which by his Ministration, was a very pleasing ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vice to him, who by pouring our of his Bloud in this Martyrdom, would confirm the Doctrine of the Gospel, or New Covenant, and fix it more strongly in the hearts of them and others of God's chosen people.</ns0:note> of your faith, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">2 Cor. 7.4.</ns0:note> I joy <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">Whereupon he expresseth his joy and delight in that, which upon this supposition would in the issue be so much to their honour and advantage, when it should seem good to the Lord. They would reckon it no small honour, to have him the Apostle that planted the Gospel amongst them satisfied in their vouching of the Truth, which therefore could not but be profitable to the establishing of them in it, who had cordially embraced it. Whereupon,</ns0:note> and rejoyce with you all <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">He doth heartily congratulate with each of them, the meanest aswell as the greatest of them, who would be so privileged.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 For the same cause also do ye joy <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Expecting the like affection and sympathy in every one of them, that upon the account of his sufferings, they would the more readily, cheerfully, and couragiously be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lieve in, and suffer for Christ. Considering the difference 'twixt death threatned by Man, for our sticking close to God, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 10.28. and denounced for slipping aside from God, in whole, or in part, 2 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 1.5.</ns0:note>, and rejoyce with me <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">And that would be a congratulation of him who should account their being established in the Faith with mutual love and unity, a fulfilling of his Faith as before, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 2.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>more<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />over</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> But I trust in the Lord Jesus <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Diverting from his former exhortation, the more to comfort them, he expresseth his good hope (which in res<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pect of the object we translate <ns0:hi>trust</ns0:hi>) in the Lord Jesus, exalted above every name, that he would be pleased some way or other, to afford him such liberty, notwithstanding his restraint.</ns0:note>, to send <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Rom. 16.21.</ns0:note> Timotheus shortly unto you <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">That he should within a little while after the arrival of <ns0:hi>Epaphroditus,</ns0:hi> now upon his return, dispatch <ns0:hi>Timothy</ns0:hi> to them.</ns0:note>, that I also may be of good comfort <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Not for their further benevolence, but for the composing of their Spirits, and setling of their af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fairs, which to him, solicitous of their Souls welfare, (as a like case for others, 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 2.19. with 3.5.) would be great satisfaction.</ns0:note>, when I know your state <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">When he should be certainly ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quainted how things went with them; who might justly expect his sympathy, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 12.15. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 12.26. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 11.28, 29.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 For I have no man <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>so dear unto me.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> like-minded <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">For which purpose I have designed <ns0:hi>Timothy</ns0:hi> who joins with me in this Epistle, and is most of the same mind with my self, endued with the same Spirit, Faith, and Love: finding none of like Soul to him with my self, in de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />siring your prosperity, and so have pitched upon him.</ns0:note>, who will naturally care for your state <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Who being cordial to me and you, will without regard to lucre, ingeniously, and sincerely, above all the rest I have here, propagate the Kingdom of Christ amongst you, and promote your Salvation in watching for your Souls, as one that must give an account, that he may do it with joy, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 13.17.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:497" />21 For all <ns0:hi>h</ns0:hi> seek their own <ns0:hi>h,</ns0:hi> not the things which are Jesus Christ's <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">So that they did postpone the glory of Christ, the safety and edification of the Church there, to their own things. Wherefore he doth not mean it <ns0:hi>absolutely,</ns0:hi> that they did not seek the things of Christ, or that they did deny Christ, for 'tis apparent, even when he penn'd this Epistle, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 1.13, 14. with <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 28.14, 15. & <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1.8. There were many that did seriously seek Christ; but <ns0:hi>com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />paratively,</ns0:hi> and in a sort, they did not seek the things of Christ so intensly as they should, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 10.24, 33. but failed as others did in other cases, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 26.58. 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 4.16. (not as if all minding of their own things were de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nied to Christ's Ministers, 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 3.4, 5. & 5.8. but) they did slip their necks from under the yoke, and did not mind the Glory of Christ in the Church of <ns0:hi>Philippi,</ns0:hi> as he did.</ns0:note>.<ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">He doth here further commend <ns0:hi>Timothy,</ns0:hi> compared with the generality of those, who with him did attend the Ministry of the Gospel at <ns0:hi>Rome,</ns0:hi> where it seems (whatever the Papists pretend) <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> did not then preside as <ns0:hi>Metro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />politan.</ns0:hi> When he saith <ns0:hi>all,</ns0:hi> he doth not necessarily imply every individual besides <ns0:hi>Timothy,</ns0:hi> (though as before, he knew not one like-minded as he was) but almost all, (as the universal sign is elsewhere <ns0:hi>Synecdochically</ns0:hi> taken, <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 6.3. <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 10.22. <ns0:hi>Mark,</ns0:hi> 1.5.) or the most part of those then employed in the Ministry, who were then at liberty, and whose inclinations (probably) he had enquired into.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Did though not <ns0:hi>simply</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>absolutely,</ns0:hi> yet <ns0:hi>after a sort,</ns0:hi> seek their own profit, ease, safety, pleasure and satisfaction, (called their <ns0:hi>own,</ns0:hi> in regard of their civil right, and the world's opinion, but yet at God's disposal, <ns0:hi>Hag.</ns0:hi> 2.8.) These they did (as <ns0:hi>Iohn,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> in another case) prefer to a long and tedious Journey for the service of Christ, unto <ns0:hi>Philippi.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 But ye know the proof of him <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">However others were found in some respects defective to the service of Christ, yet he appeals to their experience of the integrity and fidelity of <ns0:hi>Timothy</ns0:hi> in conjunction with himself, when he Preached the Gospel amongst them, and afterwards, <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 16.1, 15. & 18.5. & 19.22. & 20.4, 6.</ns0:note>, that as a son with the father <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Which he amplifies and illustrates by a <ns0:hi>Simile,</ns0:hi> when he saith, <ns0:hi>as a Son with the Father, q. d.</ns0:hi> just as a genuine and obedient Son is wont to retain the Spirit of his Father that begat him, (and <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> doth <ns0:hi>Metaphorically</ns0:hi> call <ns0:hi>Timo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thy</ns0:hi> his <ns0:hi>own</ns0:hi> Son, begotten by the Gospel, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 4.19. 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 1.1.) his dearly beloved Son, 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 1.2. and faithfull in the Lord, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 4.17. like-minded with himself, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 20.</ns0:note>, he hath served with me in the gospel <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">With whom he had not onely Preached, but served in the Gospel, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 1.1. given himself wholly to the thing. He doth not say, <ns0:hi>served me,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>under me,</ns0:hi> but <ns0:hi>with me</ns0:hi> in the Gospel, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> to advance the Glory of Christ in promoting the Gospel, by helping with <ns0:hi>Paul,</ns0:hi> and labou<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ring, working the work of the Lord, as <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> also did, and being sometime a sufferer under restraint for that service, as <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> himself, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 13.23. for the Gospel, which is not a Domination, but Ministration, wherein this great Apostle owns <ns0:hi>Timothy</ns0:hi> as his Fellow Minister.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 Him therefore I hope to send presently <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Seeing the matter was thus, he thought not of any other to employ in the service of their Faith, but hoped, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> in the Lord Jesus, as <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 19. in a short time after his present Writing, to send this excellent, humble, and ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />proved young Man, who would naturally care for their concerns, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 20.</ns0:note>, so soon as I shall see how it will go with me <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Even without any delay (though as yet to accompany <ns0:hi>Epaphroditus,</ns0:hi> he could not spare him who was so usefull to him in his bonds, to take care for things necessary to the propagation of the Gospel, in the ample City of <ns0:hi>Rome</ns0:hi>) from the hour he should come to a cer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tainty, what would be the issue of his present imprisonment, which if it should end in his being offered up, he had satisfied them before, as it would be for his own advan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tage, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 1.21. so by the Providence of God, no disservice to their Faith, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 17, 18. from which with ready submis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sion to God's will, whatever occurred, it seems he had a greater inclination to conceive a good hope of freedom</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 But <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Philem. 22.</ns0:note> I trust in the Lord <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">So he expresseth his strong perswasion as the word translate <ns0:hi>trust</ns0:hi> (being seldom used, but when the thing trusted imports the object) <ns0:hi>in the Lord, i. e.</ns0:hi> Jesus, whom he doth absolutely and eminently call Lord, being so highly exalted above all others, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 9. not onely here, but elsewhere, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 29. <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 3.1. & 4.1, 4, 10. on whom he doth wholly depend, and to whom he doth submit for the issue.</ns0:note>, that I also my self shall come shortly <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Before he had suggested his perswasion of abiding with them, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 1.25. and here that he might satisfie them he had not chang'd his mind, he adds for their comfort, that they might not be discouraged in their sufferings, what apprehensions he had after a while, of being set at liberty, (if God pleas'd) and if so, he would have them conceive, soon after he had done what was necessary at <ns0:hi>Rome,</ns0:hi> (for him who had care of all the Churches) he de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />signed to follow <ns0:hi>Timothy</ns0:hi> to them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 Yet I supposed it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">In the mean time he gives them an account why he es<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />teemed it needfull to send back <ns0:hi>Epaphroditus</ns0:hi> (whom some but without sufficient warrant would have to be the same with <ns0:hi>Epaphras, Col.</ns0:hi> 1.7. & 4.12. <ns0:hi>Philem. v.</ns0:hi> 23.) unto them, not as if he had failed in doing what he was entrusted with, but for other weighty reasons.</ns0:note>, my brother and companion in labor <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">He would have them to know he had nothing to blame him for, but all in his commen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dation, whom in the common Faith he owned to be his Christian Brother, and Fellow-helper, or Fellow-worker in the business of the Gospel, as he calls others in the like circumstances, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 16.3, 21. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 8.23. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 4.11. 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 3.2. <ns0:hi>Philem.</ns0:hi> 24.</ns0:note>, and fellow-souldier <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">And a faithfull and a constant Associate with him in the Christian warfare, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 10.4. 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 1.18. <ns0:hi>Philem.</ns0:hi> 2. under Christ their Cap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tain, against all the assaults of the Devil, and the carnal World, which are continually warring to destroy real Chris<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tianity.</ns0:note>, but <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 4.18.</ns0:note> your messen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ger <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">But your Apostle, which must be understood largely, as it is sometimes put for any Evangelist, Deacon, or Minister of the Gospel, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 16.7, 9. well rendred by us in this place, <ns0:hi>messenger</ns0:hi> compared with <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 4.18. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 8.22, 23. not being a special Apostle of Christ, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 10.2. but an Officer of the Church at <ns0:hi>Philippi,</ns0:hi> delegated by them to carry relief to <ns0:hi>Paul.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, and he that ministred to my wants <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">Unto whom it seems he did not onely deliver the present for his support according to his trust and commission, wherein he faithfully served the Church, but also as their publick Minister, greatly help <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> the Prisoner in what he stood most in need of, which <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> could not but value, being the <ns0:hi>Romans</ns0:hi> were so mild as to permit him a Captive so good attendance, and assis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tance; yet to declare his affections to the Church at <ns0:hi>Phi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lippi,</ns0:hi> he chose rather to deny himself his necessaries, than not to comfort them in remitting their faithfull Messenger so greatly desiring their welfare, with this Letter to them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 For he longed after you all <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">He gives them the <ns0:hi>first</ns0:hi> reason of his present sending, not that <ns0:hi>Epaphroditus</ns0:hi> was unwilling to stay longer with him, but because he was greatly concerned for all of them of the Church at <ns0:hi>Philippi,</ns0:hi> who had his heart as they had <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi>'s, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 1.8. & 4.1, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1.11. Solicitous to be with them to doe their Souls good.</ns0:note>, and was full of heaviness <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Especially considering their great affection to him, whom they had entrusted in this ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vice, he was in such distress for them, that his Spirits were even ready to fail him, (as <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 26.37.) from Sympathy 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 11.29.</ns0:note> because that ye had heard that he had been sick <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Knowing how much the certain report of his dangerous sickness in those circumstances, when they could understand nothing of his recovery, would affect them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 For indeed he was sick nigh unto death <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">By reason he was really taken with such a Disease, as in its own nature was mortal, and in its tendency brought him even to Death's door, as <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 38.1.</ns0:note>, but God had mercy on him <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">But God who is the great Physician, and unto whom it belongs to shew mercy unto those who address to him (without whom bodily Physicians can do nothing) by compassionating of him in his misery, was pleased to restore him to health, as 2 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 20.5, 6. But if any say, <ns0:hi>Would it not have been great mercy to have taken him from the miseries of this life, which are here prolonged?</ns0:hi> consider <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 1.21. It may be answered. 1. Death it self, as it is a privation of life, and opposite to nature, was not desirable by <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> any more than by our Saviour, but might be looked upon as a kind of misery, not to be preferred to life looked upon in it self, but with respect to another, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> as it is a passage to eternal life, so it is desirable, for that life into which it leads the Godly, and so is to be preferred to the miserable condition of this life: <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> speaks here of mercy, respecting the former, considering that this life it self is a favour of God, for the service of him, and our Neighbour. Further, 2. God's mercy here respects not onely the grievous sickness of <ns0:hi>Epaphrodi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tus,</ns0:hi> but the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>oint affliction, that the loss of him would be both to the <ns0:hi>Philippians,</ns0:hi> and to <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> in this juncture, as we may see from what follows; what Power <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> had for work<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing of Miracles, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>as chiefly to convince Infidels, and he could onely exert it when God saw good for his own Glory. Therefore he magnifies God's mercy here in a more ordi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nary way, as a return to Prayer, when he was so afflicted for his Collegues ilness, being upon an Office of kindness and compassion, his loss would be in its tendency a ground of so much sorrow to the Church, aswell as to himself.</ns0:note>: and not on him onely, but on me also <ns0:hi>c,</ns0:hi> lest I should have sorrow upon sorrow <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Whose Christianity had not extinguished his natural af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fections, but if the Church had then been bereft of <ns0:hi>Epaphro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ditus</ns0:hi> would have added the affliction for his loss, to his affliction by his suffering for Christ, it would have doubled his affliction, (yet somewhat in a different sense from that, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 1.16.) it being an ill temper not to be grieved for the affliction of the Church, <ns0:hi>Amos,</ns0:hi> 6.6. yet all our affections are to be moderated according to the will of God.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:497" />28 I sent him therefore the more carefully <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">After his recovery, without delay, denying my self the comfort of his Society, I have dispatched him away to you.</ns0:note>, that when ye see him again <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">To the end that he whom you look'd upon as dead.</ns0:note> ye may rejoice <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Might seasonably appear among you in Person, and cheer you up in your troubles for him and me.</ns0:note>, and that I may be the less sorrowfull <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">And that I, who by reason of your kindness to me, have occasioned his ab<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sence from you, might upon his safe return to you have somewhat to alleviate my grief, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 6.10.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
